entries.title: Trump signs new orders restricting birthright citizenship
entries.summary: The US president's move comes just two months after the Supreme Court ruled that his first executive order on citizenship was unconstitutional.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump signs new orders restricting birthright citizenship

August 7, 2026

The US president's move comes just two months after the Supreme Court ruled that his first executive order on citizenship was unconstitutional.

US President Donald Trump dismissed a previous Supreme Court decision on citizenship as "very unfortunate" while signing two new executive orders restricting birthright citizenship on Thursday.

"It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision," Trump said of the 6-3 vote top court ruling two months ago.

The ruling rebuked Trump's previous attempt to challenge the constitutional provision that allows individuals born on US soil automatic citizenship.  

Birthright citizenship is enshrined in the 14th ​Amendment of the US Constitution. The rule guarantees citizenship for babies born in the US with only narrow exceptions, such as the children of foreign diplomats or members of an enemy occupying force.

"This was done for a different reason. This ​was done right after the Civil War. This ‌was for the babies of slaves, and what's happening now?" Trump said on Thursday.

What are the new executive orders?

Trump's close advisor and the architect of his immigration policy, Stephen Miller, said one of the orders signed Thursday seeks to deny birthright citizenship to children of members of "foreign terrorist organizations" as well as "large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments."

Miller added that the order "ensures that large numbers of people who wrongly (would) be getting birthright citizenship will no longer be eligible for those benefits."

The second executive order targets what Trump called "birth tourism." The expression refers to visitors securing visas and traveling to the US so they would give birth while in the country, so their children are entitled to US citizenship.

"That practice of birth tourism is, as of ​the signing of this order, hereby banned. What that means is that no one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a ​visa for this ‌fraudulent purpose," Miller added.

Currently, there are no official figures depicting the number of foreigners who come to the US for the explicit purpose of giving birth to obtain citizenship. But the Trump-aligned Center for Immigration Studies claims that between 20,000-25,000 mothers did so 2016-2017.

Trump: 'Our country suffers'

The White House has argued that the new executive orders do not fall within the limits of the Supreme Court ruling.

Still, the orders are expected to be challenged in court.

"I thought we were going to win it at the Supreme Court," Trump said on Thursday. "Unfortunately, we had a bad decision, very unfair decision. Our country suffers because of it and we’re ending it a different way," Trump said.

Currently, no US law bans so-called birth tourism, but a federal regulation implemented in 2020 during Trump’s first term prohibits using temporary tourist and business visas for the primary purpose of obtaining US citizenship for a newborn.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Ebola: Africa CDC plans to use vaccine for different strain as outbreak spreads
entries.summary: The head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control pledged to deploy a vaccine for a previous Ebola strain in the current DRC outbreak, with test cases indicating a potentially live-saving level of protection.
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

The head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control pledged to deploy a vaccine for a previous Ebola strain in the current DRC outbreak, with test cases indicating a potentially live-saving level of protection.

African health authorities say they would start using a vaccine for the prior Zaire ebolavirus strain to treat the current outbreak involving a different, fast spreading strain known as Bundibugyo. The ongoing outbreak is centered in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). 

The director general of the African Centres for Disease Control, or Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, told reporters in a videoconference on Thursday that there was evidence of the vaccine eliminating deaths, if not symptoms, in the test cases conducted so far.

The Africa CDC and the World Health Organization also plan to launch research checking for a possible mutation or some other abnormality in the current outbreak, as the virus spreads at a rate six to eight times faster than any past outbreak on record.

The warnings come amid continued strikes and protests in the hardest-hit regions by some medical staff complaining either of non-payment or of inadequate pay and conditions.

What did Kaseya say about the speed of the spread?

Kaseya was speaking from Brazzaville in the neighboring Republic of Congo,after meeting with World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus in Kinshasa the previous day. 

The Africa CDC chief said authorities estimated 4,000 cases have been confirmed by now, given that 3,973 had been confirmed as of Tuesday in the latest available data. That data also pointed to 1,801 confirmed Ebola deaths. The current oubreak was only declared in mid-May and is already the second-largest on record. 

Compared to the West Africa outbreak, which took place from 2014 to 2016 and is considered the largest ever, the current strain was causing deaths 6 times faster.

"As Dr. Tedros shared with me yesterday, it's time for the WHO and Africa CDC to conduct studies to check that there is no issue, additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating, because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented," Kaseya said.

"This outbreak is just expanding."

Everyone in Ituri at risk

Kaseya said cases had now been logged in 51 health zones, compared to nine in May.

He also drew attention to the numbers of cases identified as a share of the contact tracing program's size. During the most virulent and deadly outbreak on record, the Zaire strain outbreak in DRC between 2018 and 2020, one patient was identified from every 57 contacts identified as being at risk.

Across the border in Uganda, which says it has eradicated the small number of cases it experienced this year, it had an average of one confirmed case from every 41 contacts in the list.

In DRC this year, meanwhile, there was one confirmed case for every 10 people in the contact list. Kaseya said that in his estimation, a point had been reached where anybody in the hardest-hit city of Bunia or the worst-affected region of Ituri should be considered potential contacts.

What did Kaseya say about the Zaire strain vaccine?

Doctors have had only limited chances to treat or test against the Bundibugyo Ebola strain as it had been considered rare. There are also no recognized vaccines or treatments. However, medical experts have already started working on a new jab. 

During the Thursday conference, Kaseya said that the Africa CDC planned to start dispensing an existing Ebola vaccine for the Zaire strain in the current outbreak. During limited testing, while people vaccinated against the Zaire strain did experience some symptoms, "we saw zero deaths among people who are vaccinated."

He said that this "means there is a level of protection" provided by the vaccine.

Kaseya said authorities also planned to expand the use of the antiviral drug remdesivir in affected areas.

Neighboring Uganda had reported successes treating its limited number of cases with redemsivir. It recorded 20 cases and said that only two of the patients died.

It wasn't immediately clear how many supplies of the vaccines or treatment were ready and available to dispense in a fairly remote region of the DRC that's close to active insurgencies and other forms of conflict. Africa CDC's Professor Placide Mbala said any initial rollout would be a relatively small trial. 

What's the latest on the stranded barge in Maluku near Kinshasa?

Meanwhile, authorities near the DRC capital of Kinshasa continued screening more than 300 people traveling on a river boat after the death of a passenger reported to have Ebola-like symptoms.

Health teams deployed a mobile laboratory to the vessel to conduct precautionary tests in Maluku where it was intercepted, northeast of the capital.

The city has so far avoided being exposed to the Ebola outbreak.

Kaseya on Thursday told reporters that the boat had come from Mongala province, where no Ebola cases have been reported. Prior reports had said the vessel hailed from Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province, which is an affected area. Kaseya said that initially even the government had received this erroneous information.

He said health authorities and the government nevertheless decided to screen all passengers to try to minimize risk, with results still pending.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: How drought threatens electricity supplies in Europe
entries.summary: Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are better prepared.
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are better prepared.

Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure. 

In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube.

Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria, Slovakia, Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania.

DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others.

Hungary: Most severe energy crisis in decades

No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest, and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country.

Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely.

Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity.

Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy.

Romania: Blasting rocks to redirect water

Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week.

Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch.

Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one.

Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production.

Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry — and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics.

Serbia: An unfavorable energy mix

Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower.

The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade, which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production.

Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production.

Slovakia, Austria less affected

In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought.

In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages.

Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities.

Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts.

In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources.

Bulgaria: Large battery storage capacity

Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria.

The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity.

At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity.

The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world.

These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market.

entries.title: Ceuta leader says 100 migrants died in border rush
entries.summary: With over 3,000 migrants still in Ceuta after rushing the border last week, Ceuta leader Juan Jesus Vivas warns the situation in the Spanish exclave is "unsustainable." Hundreds of those migrants are minors.
entries.content:
Spain

Ceuta leader says 100 migrants died in border rush

August 6, 2026

With over 3,000 migrants still in Ceuta after rushing the border last week, Ceuta leader Juan Jesus Vivas warns the situation in the Spanish exclave is "unsustainable." Hundreds of those migrants are minors.

Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas told EU lawmakers at the European Parliament on Thursday that some 100 people had died during last week's border surge.

He also said the city was still reeling from the event and now dealing with unaccompanied migrant minors who remain in Ceuta.

Vivas called the situation "unsustainable," and pleaded for government help.

His visit to Brussels comes a week after some 72,000 migrants rushed through the border between Morocco and Spain's North African territory of Ceuta.

The incident caused a spat between several EU countries and Madrid, with Italy suspending the Schengen free-travel pact with Spain.

On Wednesday, Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras said some 141 people had died on July 30, with 63 bodies found in Morocco and 78 in Ceuta.

Ceuta asks for more security resources

The Spanish government said that nearly all of the migrants had returned to Morocco, but Vivas noted that between 3,000 and ‌5,000 migrants were ⁠still in Ceuta.

Vivas also said Ceuta lacked the security resources necessary to deal with the situation.

"Security forces have not been deployed with the intensity required by the situation ⁠we are still facing," he told a European Parliament committee.

"Immigration services have not ⁠been sufficiently reinforced to ⁠handle the border rejections," he added.

Large number of migrant children in Ceuta

Morocco said it is ready "to work towards identifying unaccompanied ‌minors with a view to their return ‌to ​their homeland," state ​news agency MAP reported on Thursday evening, citing a diplomatic source.

It is estimated that hundreds of unaccompanied minors are currently facing limited access to food, water, shelter and sanitation in Ceuta.

Some children have been beaten and assaulted, says Jose Miguel Morales, head of Federacion Sur Acoge, a migrant rights and assistance group from southern Spain.

"Every day that passes without a solution and without safe accommodation means leaving these children — especially these girls — exposed to all kinds of abuse," he told Spanish public television.

"We are talking about real children — 10 years old or younger in some cases. Many are under 14."

Another charity, Save the Children, urged for all minors to be registered. It also warned that girls face "heightened risks of violence, trafficking and exploitation."

Minors likely to be distributed to ther parts of Spain

In 2025, after a surge of migration overwhelmed reception centers in the Canary Islands, Spain passed an immigration law reform. The new law mandated the redistribution of unaccompanied minors from overstretched territories within 15 days of their case file being completed.

However, the redistribution of the children to the rest of Spain is expected to meet resistance from regions governed by the center-right Popular Party (PP) and the anti-immigration, far-right Vox party.

But Spain's socialist government already has warned against the pushback, with Deputy Prime Minister Carlos Cuerpo saying that PP and its regional governments "must comply with the law just like everyone else."

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Germany news: Officials deny reports of drone near munitions-laden plane
entries.summary: Officials in Germany have rejected reports that an explosive-laden drone found at Leipzig airport was next to a plane filled with weapons destined for Ukraine. Federal prosecutors have taken over the case. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Officials deny reports of drone near munitions-laden plane

Published August 6, 2026last updated August 6, 2026

Officials in Germany have rejected reports that an explosive-laden drone found at Leipzig airport was next to a plane filled with weapons destined for Ukraine. Federal prosecutors have taken over the case. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Officials reject reports of drone with explosive charge near plane with munitions for Ukraine
  • Several German media outlets had previously said the aircraft at Leipzig airport was packed with weapons
  • Federal prosecutors take over Leipzig airport drone investigation
  • An investigation team is searching for a possible second drone that is believed to have hit a plane midair
  • Western officials have repeatedly accused Russia and its proxies of staging attacks and other incidents across Europe
  • A public health agency said nearly 12,000 people in Germany have died of heat-related causes this summer

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Thursday, August 6, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Two suspected IS members detained in NRW

Two suspected IS members detained in NRW

Two Iraqi nationals have been arrested on suspicion of terrorism by German authorities. The arrests took place after evidence emerged that they had fought with the so-called Islamic State in Iraq a decade ago. 

The arrests were made in the towns of Höxter and Bottrop in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Cell phones and laptops were seized from the detainees' apartments.

The men, aged 29 and 46, have been accused of being members of a terrorist organization abroad, a spokeswoman for the Düsseldorf State Prosecutor's Office said. She added that the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) received a tip and was then able to track down the suspects.

Authorities have not yet decided whether the men would be held in pretrial detention.

There are no indications that either of them was involved in any planned attacks in Germany, the spokeswoman added.

Skip next section RWE settles with Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects in US

RWE settles with Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects in US

German energy giant RWE announced it is abandoning its offshore wind power projects in the US, citing regulatory hurdles, and turning towards investments elsewhere. 

The company said in a statement that it had reached a $1.22 billion (roughly €1.05 billion) settlement with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases in the New York Bight and off the coasts of Louisiana and California.

"After careful consideration, it was determined that there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future," RWE said.

The company said it now planned to reinvest the money in natural gas projects in the US "to meet rapidly growing energy demand" instead of focusing on wind turbines and renewable energy. 

US President Donald Trump, who has become a vocal supporter of the fossil fuel industry, seems to reserve a particular distaste for what he typically calls "windmills."

Last week he returned to the issue in comments related to the UK, saying "any time you see windmills, you see a failing country," and claiming — falsely on both counts: "They're all made in China. They're not used by China, but they're made in China."

RWE said it was still investing in its US operations and aiming to almost double its power generation capacity by 2031. It also noted its continued heavy presence in offshore wind projects beyond Germany's borders.

Skip next section UPDATE — Cologne WWII Rhine riverbed bomb successfully defused

UPDATE — Cologne WWII Rhine riverbed bomb successfully defused

By early evening on Thursday, several hours after work started to clear the exclusion zone, Cologne authorities said the World War II bomb uncovered amid low Rhine River levels no longer posed a threat. 

"Experts from the regional government in Düsseldorf's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Service have just successfully disarmed the bomb," Cologne's city administration said.

"The barriers are now being gradually lifted; residents can return to their apartments, as can the residents who were evacuated at the old people's home on the Konrad Adenauer bank."

The exclusion zone also included the headquarters of national private broadcaster RTL. RTL's evening news bulletin, which aired just over an hour ago, was recorded from their studio in the capital, Berlin, instead. Its rolling news channel, ntv, had been producing afternoon programming from a mobile studio.

Skip next section Federal prosecutors take over Leipzig airport drone investigation

Federal prosecutors take over Leipzig airport drone investigation

Federal prosecutors in Germany have confirmed that they will take over investigations of the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, given the grounds to suspect a dangerous attempt to attack air transport and cause an explosion.

"To this end, professional explosives and a detonator were attached to the drone," the federal prosecutor's office said. Beyond that, it noted there was evidence suggesting a mid-air collision between a plane and possibly another drone.

"This is a serious attack on transport and logistical infrastructure in Germany," the Office of the Federal Prosecutor said as it announced it was taking the lead. "As such, the act is capable of undermining the external and internal security of the Federal Republic of Germany."

Prosecutors said the federal investigative police force, the BKA, would take over the policing side of the case.

Prior to this announcement, the Dresden public prosecutor's office and the Saxony state chapter of the investigative police force had been conducting the investigation.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt had already said on Wednesday evening that the attempted attack seemed to be the work of highly trained professionals and that he did not rule out the possibility of "foreign powers" being involved in some way. 

Skip next section Chinese EV makers get most out of Germany subsidy

Chinese EV makers get most out of Germany subsidy

Chinese manufacturers benefited from the introduction of the German government's new electric car subsidy.

The €3 billion ($3.46 billion) subsidy scheme was introduced by Germany's conservative-led coalition government to incentivize consumers to purchase and lease electric cars, certain plug-in hybrids and EVs fitted with range extenders.

According to the Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA), the Chinese manufacturer BYD was one of those who benefited. BYD registered sales of 5,240 new cars in Germany in July, more than four and a half times as many cars in July of the previous year.

"While the strong growth in electric cars is accelerating the ramp-up of electromobility in Germany, it has so far brought only limited benefits to the domestic automotive industry," said auto expert Constantin Gall of the consulting firm EY, adding that Chinese companies are the main beneficiaries.

The high demand for electric cars has been a boost for the entire new-car market in Germany.

Skip next section Officials deny explosive drone was near plane carrying weapons for Ukraine, media report

Officials deny explosive drone was near plane carrying weapons for Ukraine, media report

The German Interior Ministry has denied reports that a drone carrying explosives was near a cargo aircraft packed with munitions destined for Ukraine, according to media reports.

In a meeting of the heads of the Bundestag's committees for Defense and Interior Affairs, it was made clear that no weapons or other munitions were on the aircraft, according to the dpa news agency, which reported information matching an earlier article by the Focus news magazine (see earlier entry).

Detlef Seif, the chair of the Internal Affairs Committee, also rejected the reports, telling Reuters that from all the conversations he was party to so far, "the aircraft was not loaded with ammunition or weapons."

Maret Montavon, head of communications and government relations at Mitteldeutsche Flughafen, which operates the airport in Leipzig, told the daily Leipziger Volkszeitung that there was no cargo on the aircraft.

"The Antonov aircraft in question was empty at the time of the incident and, therefore, carried no cargo. This assessment is consistent with the information we have received from Antonov Logistics SALIS," Montavon told the paper.

The ministry has not responded to an official request for comment.

Security sources have said a drone carrying explosives was located on Tuesday near a Ukrainian Antonov AN-124 Condor cargo aircraft. Federal Police defused the explosive device.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is inviting several European counterparts to a meeting following the incident, his ministry confirmed on Thursday. The meeting will aim to coordinate a joint defense strategy to combat drones and to improve the protection of critical infrastructure.

Skip next section Rare Focke-Wulf 190 aircraft back in sky after restoration in Turkey

Rare Focke-Wulf 190 aircraft back in sky after restoration in Turkey

Turkey's Sivrihisar Aviation Club Association has successfully restored a rare German World War II Focke-Wulf 190 (FW 190) fighter plane and returned it to the skies.

German pilot Klaus Plasa was at the controls for its flight earlier in the week.

The FW 190 went into service in 1941 and was a heavier plane than its better-known counterpart, the Messerschmitt Bf 109, and less comfortable at high altitudes. But this also made it a much more versatile aircraft, capable of flying longer distances and carrying more firepower and fuel.

The aircraft was downed in France in 1944. Its wreckage was taken to the US in 2000. Restoration work began there, but the aircraft never regained operational status.

The Turkish aviation club acquired the plane in 2023 and an 11-member team set to work restoring it over roughly 14 months.

In the early 20th century, Germany had helped modernize the military, including the air force, of what was then the Ottoman Empire. This collaboration continued in the early years of the Republic of Turkey.

By 1948, three years after Nazi Germany's defeat and with spare parts in short supply, Turkey — which by then was starting to eye an alliance with the US and membership in what would become NATO — retired its remaining FW 190 fleet.

The Sivrihisar Aviation Club Association said it wanted to preserve the countries' shared aviation heritage. It plans to display the rare aircraft at an air show in Eskisehir in September.

Estimates on the numbers vary, but no more than a few dozen FW 190s survive, most of them museum pieces that are not airworthy.

Skip next section Gelsenkirchen tram accident leaves 25 injured, 10 seriously

Gelsenkirchen tram accident leaves 25 injured, 10 seriously

Two trams have collided in the western city of Gelsenkirchen.

Local newspaper the Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung (WAZ) based in nearby Essen carried the first images of two trams that appeared to have collided end-to-end. 

The crash took place on Kurt-Schumacher-Strasse near Bundesliga club Schalke's Veltins-Arena.

"As things stand, seven of the 25 people involved are seriously injured, and three are in a life-threatening condition," a police spokesperson said, according to the DPA news agency.

Traffic was suspended in both directions at the scene as emergency services responded. The incident was first reported at around 12:30 p.m. local time.

The police spokesperson also said one of the trains, which was conducting driver training, stopped and the other then crashed into it from behind. The cause of the incident was under investigation.

Skip next section Low Rhine River level reveals WWII bomb in central Cologne

Low Rhine River level reveals WWII bomb in central Cologne

Authorities in Cologne were working to defuse or dispose of an unexploded World War II bomb, revealed as the Rhine River's water levels sink to record lows in the hot and dry summer.

The operation took place in the central Deutz district, just across the river from the main train station and Cologne's renowned cathedral. 

The discovery of the US bomb led to efforts to clear a safe zone in a radius of roughly 400 meters from the scene. Around 360 people were affected, city authorities said. 

One of central Cologne's green spaces, the Rheinpark on the right bank of the river, was cleared amid the operation.

By mid-afternoon, the City of Cologne published a list of areas that were cordoned off, asking people to stay clear.

It had said slightly earlier that it was not yet possible to say when the bomb would be defused or otherwise rendered safe.

Such finds are very common occurrences in Cologne, a strategically important city that was heavily bombed throughout much of World War II. Most of the bombs can be defused or disabled; a minority require a controlled explosion instead. 

High temperatures and a lack of rain have often led to the summertime discovery of unexploded bombs in German rivers. 

Skip next section READ — Leipzig explosive drone was next to plane with munitions for Ukraine

READ — Leipzig explosive drone was next to plane with munitions for Ukraine

German regional public broadcasters WDR and NDR, and the Süddeutsche Zeitung daily, report that the drone found at Leipzig airport had been placed next to a cargo plane set to carry munitions to Ukraine.

They're citing an internal police report to which they have access.

However, according to the magazine Focus, citing participants in a Bundestag committee meeting, the Interior Ministry said there had been no ammunition on board the aircraft and that the last such transport flight had taken place on July 29.

Federal authorities have already opened a terrorism investigation into the case.

For more details on this and the overall investigation, check out this feature by Marcel Fürstenau from our politics desk. 

Skip next section Germany's heat death toll rises to nearly 12,000

Germany's heat death toll rises to nearly 12,000

Nearly 12,000 people have died from the effects of extreme heat in Germany this year, according to new estimates from the Robert Koch Institute.

The German public health institute put the number of heat-related deaths between April 6 and July 26 at around 11,900, already well above any full-year total since 2016.

The previous annual high was around 9,000 deaths in 2018.

Around 9,600 of this year's deaths were linked to the exceptionally hot week from June 22 to 28.

Average temperatures across Germany reached 26.4 degrees Celsius (79.5 degrees Fahrenheit) that week, while daytime temperatures topped 40 degrees C (104 degrees F) in many places.

The institute described the latest total as a conservative estimate, meaning the true figure could be higher.

People aged 85 and above accounted for around 6,000 deaths, while almost 3,000 victims were aged between 75 and 84.

Around 1,800 deaths were recorded among people aged 65 to 74, while about 1,100 were among those younger than 65.

Heat rarely kills directly. More often, extreme temperatures worsen existing illnesses or put additional strain on the cardiovascular system.

Skip next section Munich car-ramming attacker sentenced to life in prison

Munich car-ramming attacker sentenced to life in prison

A German court has sentenced Farhad N. to life in prison for murder and attempted murder over a deadly car attack on a Verdi trade union demonstration in Munich.

A 37-year-old mother and her two-year-old child were killed in the February 2025 attack, while more than 40 people were injured.

Skip next section Germany arrests Ukrainian suspected of spying on a defense company in Bavaria

Germany arrests Ukrainian suspected of spying on a defense company in Bavaria

German authorities have arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying on a defense company in Bavaria to prepare possible acts of sabotage.

Investigators suspect he took photographs of the premises of a Bavarian defense company in June and passed them to handlers working for a foreign intelligence service.

Skip next section Industry demands action ahead of low-water talks

Industry demands action ahead of low-water talks

Ahead of Thursday's crisis talks in Bonn over exceptionally low river water levels, German industry and shipping groups are demanding concrete measures, including deepenening the river at certain points.

Holger Lösch, deputy managing director of the Federation of German Industries, told the Rheinische Post newspaper that selective deepening would allow ships to carry more cargo during periods of low water and make supply chains more resilient.

"The low-water conference in Bonn must mark the starting point for accelerating targeted deepening of the Rhine," said Lösch.

Lösch also called for more investment in waterways, arguing that Germany's transport infrastructure had been underfunded for decades.

He said planning and approval procedures also needed to be sped up significantly.

Germany's inland shipping association likewise urged the government to act.

"It is high time that the importance of rivers and canals for Germany as a business location is recognized and given greater priority."

Schwanen criticized decades of delays, noting that improving navigability of the Middle and Lower Rhine has been listed as an urgent priority in Germany's federal transport infrastructure plan since 1992.

"It is shameful that the federal government has intended for 34 years to do something for freight shipping and its customers without all that much happening," he said.

Skip next section Germany calls crisis talks over extreme low river levels

Germany calls crisis talks over extreme low river levels

German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger is holding high-level talks in Bonn today as extreme low water levels disrupt shipping on the Rhine and other rivers.

Representatives from the shipping industry, ports and businesses are due to attend the meeting around lunchtime.

"We want to assess the current situation together and take short-term action where necessary," Bilger told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper ahead of the talks.

He said the government also wanted to draw longer-term lessons and make Germany's waterways more resilient to increasingly severe periods of low water.

Bilger is due to speak to reporters immediately after the meeting.

Low water levels are forcing inland cargo vessels to carry significantly lighter loads, pushing up transport costs and putting particular pressure on industries that rely on bulk freight.

entries.title: The Mata Hari affair: Courtesan, spy, legend
entries.summary: Regarded the most famous female spy of all time, dancer Mata Hari had men falling at her feet — but was executed for treason. Did she really betray state secrets?
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

Regarded the most famous female spy of all time, dancer Mata Hari had men falling at her feet — but was executed for treason. Did she really betray state secrets?

Mata Hari was already a legend in her own lifetime. When she stepped into the Parisian limelight in 1905, she swept high society off its feet.

"She danced with veils and jewel-encrusted bustiers and almost nothing else," the Parisian press reported. "Never had anyone dared to appear unveiled before the gods with such trembling ecstasy. And what wonderful movements she made — both daring and demure at the same time."

Mata Hari had convinced audiences and the press that she was an exotic temple dancer — but the dark-haired performer was actually Dutch.

One of the hallmarks of the Belle Époque era was a heightened fascination with cultures the Parisians deemed to be exotic. Driven by financial desperation, she exploited this demand by pretending to be Indian. To make her act more credible, she fabricated a backstory claiming to be the daughter of a highly esteemed Brahmin. 

"My mother, first bayadere [dancer] of the Ranganathaswamy Temple, died at the age of fourteen, on the day I was born. After the temple priests cremated her body, they adopted me and named me Mata Hari, which means 'Eye of the Day [a Malay word, Hari means sun]."

She claimed to have learned the sacred temple dances from a young age. During her performances, one veil after another would fall away. Later, she said, "I never danced well. The only reason people came to see me was that I was the first to dare to present myself naked to the public."

From Dutch hatmaker's daughter to Mata Hari

High society couldn't get enough of Mata Hari, unaware that her real name was Margaretha Geertruida Zelle and that she came from the small Dutch town of Leeuwarden.

Born on August 7, 1876, Mata Hari was the daughter of a hatmaker who had become wealthy through stock market speculation. He often spoiled his daughter with lavish gifts. For her sixth birthday, he gave her a carriage drawn by goats.

At the age of 13, Mata Hari's life of luxury ended abruptly. Her father went bankrupt and abandoned the family. Two years later, when her mother passed away, she moved in with relatives. Eventually, she met her husband through a newspaper ad: "An officer from the Dutch East Indies [now Indonesia], currently on home leave, seeks the company of a nice young woman with potential for future marriage. Financial circumstances irrelevant." 

Mata Hari and John Rudolf MacLeod, a Dutch nobleman of Scottish descent who was 20 years her senior, quickly became a couple. In 1897, she accompanied her husband to the Dutch East Indies. But her dream of a happy life never materialized. Frequent arguments strained their relationship. Then, their two-year-old son was tragically poisoned to death. When the MacLeods returned to Europe in 1902, their marriage fell apart. MacLeod left Mata Hari, taking their daughter with him and refusing to pay any alimony, leaving her to fend for herself.

She began her career in Paris as a model for painters and tried her luck at the circus.  But it was her creation of the exotic stage persona Mata Hari that ultimately made her famous. She performed at prestigious venues across Europe, including Vienna and Monte Carlo, staying in luxurious hotels.  She danced at soirées hosted by the Rothschild banking family and entertained Crown Prince Wilhelm, the son of the German Emperor Wilhelm II. Her success gave her access to the highest social circles, where she formed relationships with diplomats and high-ranking military officers who paid generously for her company.

World War I agent driven by financial hardship

Eventually, Mata Hari's popularity began to wane. Younger dancers began imitating her, and thrill-seeking audiences in Paris moved on to the next sensation. When World War I broke out in 1914, Mata Hari could no longer sustain her luxurious lifestyle. 

She accepted an offer from the German consul in the Netherlands to help pay off her debts. She was promised even more money for gathering intelligence from influential figures on the opposing side of the war. Her initial fee was 20,000 francs, a substantial sum at the time. And just like that, she became Agent H 21.

Then, when the French intelligence service approached her and offered her even more money, Mata Hari became a double agent. But she miscalculated the situation. The French had enlisted her so they could catch her spying for the Germans. At the same time, due to increasing suspicion of her activities, the British intelligence service also monitored Mata Hari as she traveled through Europe. On February 13, 1917, she was arrested.

On October 15, at the age of 41, Mata Hari was executed for high treason in the moat of the Château de Vincennes, near Paris. Eyewitnesses reported that she faced the 12-man firing squad with her head held high and even blew them a kiss. She refused to wear a blindfold and instead addressed her final words to the commander who gave the order to fire: "Thank you, monsieur!"

Mata Hari's status as a so-called master spy remains questionable. According to documents from the British intelligence service — which remained classified for several decades — any information she may have shared likely did not impact the course of World War I.

It seems that Mata Hari was used as a convenient scapegoat at a time when public enthusiasm for the war had significantly waned. And the French military court needed someone to blame. She herself denied having spied until the very end. Regardless of whether or not she was a master spy, she was undoubtedly a master of self-promotion until her last breath.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?
entries.summary: UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?
entries.content:
Cyprus

Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?

August 6, 2026

UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres last week became the first UN chief to visit Cyprus in 16 years.

While there, he met the leaders of the island's two communities: Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Tufan Erhurman, Turkish Cypriot leader and president of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is only recognized by Turkey.

His aim in doing so was to determine whether the conditions exist for restarting negotiations on the Cyprus issue.

Progress on talks has remained stalled since the collapse of negotiations in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, in 2017, when the United Nations made its most comprehensive effort to broker a reunification agreement for the island.

Why now?

So, why has Antonio Guterres decided to launch a new initiative now?

According to diplomatic sources, the answer lies less in developments surrounding the Cyprus issue itself and more in the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape of the wider region.

War in the Middle East, deteriorating relations between Israel and Turkey, and growing strategic competition in the Eastern Mediterranean have heightened UN concerns that the unresolved Cyprus conflict could undermine the stability of the entire region.

Guterres said as much after the joint meeting on July 29. "I do believe that a solution in Cyprus is absolutely crucial, not only to preserve the interests and the peace of the Cyprus people, but also as a factor of stability in what is becoming a dangerously unstable region," he said.

Speaking to DW, Andreas Mavroyiannis, former permanent representative of the Republic of Cyprus to the United Nations and former chief negotiator of the Greek Cypriot side, shared the same concern.

"The strengthening of relations between the Republic of Cyprus and Israel, combined with the deterioration of Israel–Turkey relations, increases the risk of the Cyprus issue being instrumentalized," he told DW.

According to Mavroyiannis, the UN secretary-general fears that Cyprus could, instead of serving as a pillar of stability in the Middle East, become increasingly entangled in regional rivalries and emerge as one of the area's most vulnerable flashpoints.

The European dimension

The UN is not alone in viewing the Cyprus issue through the prism of regional security. The EU has also shown increasing interest in playing a more active political role in efforts to revive the peace process.

A significant step came on July 7, when the European Commission appointed Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's Special Representative for the Cyprus issue.

His mandate is to support the UN-led process and strengthen the bloc's involvement in efforts to restart negotiations.

A more active role for the EU has long been one of President Nikos Christodoulides' key policy objectives.

During Cyprus' recent presidency of the Council of the European Union, he reminded fellow European leaders that he was "the president of the only EU member state that remains under illegal military occupation."

The Cypriot government believes that the EU agenda could provide Ankara with incentives to contribute constructively to progress on the Cyprus issue.

Among the issues viewed as potential leverage are the modernization of the EU–Turkey Customs Union, visa liberalization for Turkish citizens, Turkey's participation in the EU's SAFE defense financing instrument and the prospect of gradually reviving its long-frozen EU accession process.

The next step

While Guterres' decision to announce a new informal expanded 5+1 meeting involving the two Cypriot communities, the three guarantor powers (Greece, Turkey and the UK) plus the UN was widely seen as a positive signal, he deliberately stopped short of setting a date.

Instead, he made it clear that the meeting would only be convened once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process.

So, it was no coincidence that he stressed upon arriving in Cyprus that "it depends obviously on the Cypriots themselves," underlining that responsibility for moving the process forward rests primarily with the two communities.

His remarks are directly linked to the lack of tangible progress on confidence-building measures.

Despite months of discussions, the two sides failed to reach agreement even on the opening of new crossing points — a step which, according to the UN Secretary-General, could have "a tangible impact on the daily lives of Cypriots," while helping to restore a minimum level of trust ahead of the next phase of negotiations.

Ankara's position remains crucial

The key question, however, extends beyond the two communities themselves and concerns Turkey's willingness to engage.

The real test for the UN is whether Ankara is prepared to return to negotiations conducted within the framework of the UN Security Council resolutions and the agreed basis of a bicommunal, bizonal federation, moving away from the two-state solution it has advocated since the collapse of the Crans-Montana talks in 2017.

So far, Turkey has made no public statement indicating such a shift. The only possible indication comes indirectly from Antonio Guterres' remark that he has "the consent of both sides and the guarantor powers to move towards another 5+1 meeting, provided there is adequate preparation."

The wording suggests that, at least procedurally, Ankara is willing to participate in another informal conference under UN auspices. Whether this also signals a substantive change in Turkey's long-standing position remains, for now, an open question.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Why Iran is sending mixed signals on talks
entries.summary: Trump says talks with Iran are underway. Tehran says it is discussing the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, not Washington. Analysts say the gap reflects competing political pressures.
entries.content:
Iran

Why Iran is sending mixed signals on talks

August 6, 2026

Trump says talks with Iran are underway. Tehran says it is discussing the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, not Washington. Analysts say the gap reflects competing political pressures.

US President Donald Trump on Monday said that negotiations with Iran were ongoing over the Strait of Hormuz, adding that the Islamic Republic was facing a "last chance before decapitation." 

Trump told reporters at the White House that he agreed to continue to pursue talks with Iran at the request of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.

His remarks appeared to contradict public statements from Tehran, which has so far denied that negotiations with Washington were taking place.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei nevertheless confirmed that Tehran was holding talks with Oman over the strategic waterway. 

The two sides may therefore be describing the same diplomatic channel in different terms, each using language aimed at its own domestic audience.

Washington describes the Omani mediation as negotiations with Iran. Tehran portrays it as a technical discussion with Oman about shipping through the strait.

Hormuz remains the main obstacle

The Strait of Hormuz has become the main sticking point.

Commercial traffic through key waterway remains severely restricted, while ships continue to face attacks near the strait.

According to data from maritime analytics company Kpler cited by Reuters news agency, only six commercial vessels crossed the route on Monday, down from seven the previous day.

The uncertainty surrounding the key waterway has also affected global markets.

Hopes of diplomatic progress recently pushed oil prices lower and helped stock markets rise. But those movements reflected how sensitive markets remain to any news about the strait, rather than evidence that the crisis had been resolved.

Iran wants some measure of control over vessels entering the Persian Gulf to be recognized. The United States wants the strait fully reopened to unrestricted international shipping.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW that the disagreement is no longer simply about whether the two sides are talking.

"The question is what to call those talks and what each side hopes to gain from them," he said.

Trump describes the indirect channel as negotiations because he needs to show that military and economic pressure has brought Tehran back to the table, Dorbeiki said.

He suggested that Iran avoids the same terminology because acknowledging negotiations with Washington could be seen by its domestic opponents as surrender.

The two sides remain far apart.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki said. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Divisions inside Iran

The contradictory messages also reflect divisions between rival political factions inside Iran.

Dorbeiki identifies two broad camps.

"The first, which could be described as the 'development and reconstruction through agreement' camp, believes that without sanctions relief and the reopening of Hormuz, Iran's economy cannot recover or even sustain itself," he told DW.

According to Dorbeiki, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and some Revolutionary Guard figures with economic interests may be closer to that view.

The opposing camp, which includes the Paydari Front, a small, ultra-conservative party, "sees an agreement with the United States as an ideological defeat" and favors continued resistance.

Leadership vacuum adds to uncertainty

The lack of a clear leader in Iran has added to the uncertainty.

Since the country's then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was killed in an airstrike on February 28 the first hours of the US-Israeli war against Iran, authority has become more fragmented.

His son Mojtaba Khamenei was named new supreme leader, but his role remains unclear and he has not been seen in public since the war began amid speculation he was severely injured in the strike.

Dorbeiki says this has allowed rival groups to claim they speak for the leadership.

"Indirect talks through Oman are likely to continue," he told DW. "Pezeshkian will remain under pressure, but he is unlikely to be removed for now because the domestic and international political costs would be high."

Dorbeiki noted that keeping Pezeshkian in office leaves open the option of blaming him if the negotiations fail.

Three competing camps inside Iran

Hassan Asadi Zeidabadi, an Iranian political analyst based in Tehran, believes the main decision-makers in Tehran have already accepted the need for negotiations.

However, he says there are three main camps within the Iranian establishment.

The first consists of government officials dealing with the economic effects of the war and blockade, making them more inclined toward negotiations.

"The second group is made up mainly of military figures who want to improve their position in the conflict before negotiating and remain skeptical of US intentions," Zeidabadi told DW.

"The third group is made up of ideological hardliners who believe that reaching an agreement with Washington after the war and the killing of Iran's supreme leader would mark the end of the Islamic Republic's traditional identity, which is rooted in opposition to the West."

"They fear the day after an agreement," Asadi Zeidabadi added. "For them, a deal with the United States would mean the end of the ideological era they represent and, ultimately, their own removal."

Zeidabadi said these hardliners retain influence in parliament, the security establishment and the state's propaganda apparatus, and fear the changes a deal could bring.

The future of the talks may depend less on Muscat or Washington than on which factions gain the upper hand in Tehran.

If supporters of an agreement convince the leadership that continued isolation threatens reconstruction, the economy and ultimately the system's survival, diplomacy could move forward.

If hardliners succeed in presenting any compromise as surrender, even the indirect talks could collapse.

Based on the positions outlined by both analysts, further reports of progress are likely to be accompanied by contradictory public statements.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: AfD threatens to cut funding for 'modern-thinking' culture
entries.summary: The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.

In upcoming state elections to be held on September 6, polls suggest the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could win an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Based on the far-right's cultural policy program, museums, theaters and cultural institutions in the region say that artistic freedom is one of the far-right party's targets.

The AfD has announced that artists and institutions would be required to sign a declaration pledging "not to hold in contempt Germany and its culture" if they want to obtain state funding. Many of these organizations and individuals heavily rely on these subsidies.

The AfD's interpretation of disrespect to German culture also ambiguously includes what the party calls "anti-German art."

"We declared in our government program that we no longer intend to spend public funds on promoting anti-German art," said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD parliamentary group in the state legislature, in a speech held in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament in late June.

Asked by other members of parliament to specify what that meant exactly, Tillschneider said, "Anti-German art is German art that doesn't want to be German." He mentioned as an example an opera production he had seen some years ago; the classical German composer's work was revisited through a "feminist deconstructivist" lens that didn't please him and corresponds to what he sees as "anti-German art."

"This anti-German aversion is still considered de rigueur in large parts of the theater world," he said. "We will no longer support this attitude — let me state that quite clearly."

Bauhaus, a direct target — like in the 1930s

Bauhaus, Germany's iconic architecture, art and design school founded in 1919, was forced to close under the Nazis, who considered their avant-garde ideas and their open-minded attitude to be "un-German." Bauhaus nevertheless went on to become one of design's most important movements of the 20th century; its influence is still felt worldwide. 

Today, the AfD once again sees Bauhaus as too modernist and globalist for the "patriotic cultural policy" the party envisions.

"The AfD's criticism of Bauhaus picks up on criticism from 100 years ago; their wording is similar," Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation, told DW.

The AfD Saxony-Anhalt's program describes Bauhaus as "a controversial school of architecture" and criticizes the current state government for putting too much emphasis on this landmark attraction in their current image campaign, titled "moderndenken" (thinking modern).

The AfD aims to adopt instead a campaign called "deutschdenken" (thinking German), which would downplay the role of Bauhaus and instead "highlight the state's significant contributions to the development of the German nation — from Henry I and Otto I to Luther, Bismarck and Nietzsche."

Historically loaded language

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) strongly rejects comparisons to the Nazi party and Adolf Hitler, often dismissing them as trivializations of Nazi crimes.

Yet in its cultural policy program, the far-right party regularly adopts the language used in Hitler's propaganda, downplays Nazi-era atrocities, challenges Germany's culture of remembrance and uses historically loaded language.

The proposed "deutschdenken" slogan is one example of this: "'Deutsch denken' refers to a speech Adolf Hitler made in 1938" — the "Reichenberger Rede," noted Steiner.

Culture needs state support to thrive

The Bauhaus is not the only cultural organization that feels threatened in Saxony-Anhalt. "As cultural practitioners, cultural initiators and artists, we can say that we are now genuinely afraid, because what's being triggered there is, in fact, the idea that art and culture must be 'German,'" Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum Magdeburg told DW.

Laabs is a spokesperson for the initiative Kultur ist Vielfalt und Heimat, which roughly translates as "Culture is diversity and home." The initiative brings together a wide range of cultural institutions and artists from the region; they are warning in a joint statement that the AfD's plans could have far-reaching consequences for artistic freedom, historical memory, and public cultural life.

"We all know that what we do — from theaters to museums to libraries — is paid for with taxpayer money. It wouldn't exist otherwise," said Laabs.

Restricting funding based on an arbitrary definition of what constitutes "German" art basically equates to culture's demise, explains Laabs: "If we look at the bigger picture, we see that culture and art have been free for centuries and have known no boundaries — not even national ones. Wherever there are national boundaries, there is no longer any art or culture worthy of that name."

'Resist the beginnings'

Along with threats to funding, the AfD's program also describes Germany's existing culture of Holocaust remembrance as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" that has "blocked the possibilities for forming a stable national identity." It sees this as an "identity disorder" that needs to be "healed," by focusing on the "positive aspects of German history."

Sabine Schramm, director of Magdeburg's puppet theater, finds "it regrettable that we humans are not willing to draw conclusions from a complex history — conclusions that matter both to us as individuals and to us as a society."

She notes that throughout her 30-year career in theater, she has dealt with Germany's culture of remembrance, grappling with the horrors of Nazism on stage.

"It has always been important to me — especially in productions for young people — to tell stories that address precisely this issue: National Socialism, how it begins, and how the various elements interlock," she points out.

"I can still see myself standing on stage talking about 'resisting the beginnings' — that phrase, 'resisting the beginnings,' has become such a cliché," she says, referring to an idea Germans are deeply familiar with; after the horrors of the Nazi era, the generations that followed were urged to speak out against threats to democracy — before it's too late.

"But where, exactly, are the beginnings?" Schramm asks. "Is this the beginning, or are we still before the beginning? Are we right in the middle of it? What must I do to resist the beginnings?"

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Germany: Leipzig airport drone attack sets off alarm bells
entries.summary: German authorities have begun a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into a drone laden with explosives found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. It is seen as a "hybrid attack scenario."
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Leipzig airport drone attack sets off alarm bells

August 6, 2026

German authorities have begun a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into a drone laden with explosives found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. It is seen as a "hybrid attack scenario."

German airports have seen hundreds of drone alerts, but this incident eclipses them all: in the middle of the night on Wednesday, airport staff at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in the eastern state of Saxony found a drone rigged with explosives on the runway.

Federal police specialists were able to defuse it using a bomb disposal robot. The incident prompted the closure of part of one of Europe's largest cargo hubs.

German media reports say that experts from Saxony state police found the package to contain the highly explosive substances PETN and Semtex, which are also used in military applications. The detonator attached to the package had apparently broken off, which prevented an explosion.

A hybrid threat scenario

This unconfirmed information is particularly significant because the drone was found next to a plane of the Ukrainian state-owned carrier Antonov Airlines. The aircraft was reportedly loaded with military munitions that — according to reports — had just been transported from France to Leipzig and were slated for onward shipment to Ukraine.

Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cut his vacation short to assess the situation firsthand at the scene. His initial assessment: "This represents a new threat scenario." At a press conference on Wednesday evening, he spoke only in general and vague terms regarding potential perpetrators and motives. However, Dobrindt did not rule out the possibility that "foreign powers" might be behind the incident — with the aim of unsettling Germany.

"All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said.

In June, Dobrindt created a so-called Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, as Germany has been on high alert for espionage, sabotage and disinformation, particularly from Russia.

Suspecting links to Russia

Leipzig/Halle Airport is high on the priority list regarding security and, like other airports, is being equipped with technology to detect and intercept drones. At the same time, however, Dobrindt acknowledged that this is an ongoing race: "When drones are designed to bypass technology, the technology itself must be continuously upgraded," he said.

After Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig/Halle Airport is Germany's largest cargo hub. Security experts say this makes it a potential target for state-sponsored attacks. Consequently, counter-terrorism expert Hans-Jakob Schindler considers it possible that Russia could be the mastermind behind the explosive-laden drone.

For the moment, the facts remain unknown. "But given the location — where we have already seen similar disruptions that could be traced back to Russia — that would be my initial assumption," Schindler told DW.

Hybrid attacks generally refer to covert operations that do not aim for direct confrontation, but are designed to create uncertainty. These can involve a combination of various tactics such as sabotage, economic pressure, or disinformation.

Earlier on Thursday, Saxony's Interior Minister Armin Schuster said that authorities are searching for parts of a possible second drone that collided with an aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport.

Germany's anti-drone defense in the spotlight

Drone sightings have frequently disrupted German airports, canceling flights and causing headaches for travelers. Drones are also sometimes sighted over German military installations.

In December last year, Holger Münch, the head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), said that over 1,000 suspicious drones had been registered in 2025, which he said represented a "significant situation of danger."

Leipzig had already been the site of an attempted attack in July 2024: a container belonging to the logistics company DHL caught fire in the airport's cargo area. The cause was a package sent from the Baltic states containing an incendiary device designed — according to investigators — to detonate mid-air. At the time, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office suspected a targeted act of Russian sabotage.

This article was translated from German.
